# Scoring people {#scoring}

<div class="goals">
**Learning goals.** After this chapter you can

* compare EAP, MAP, ML and WLE scores and say when each is a sensible
  choice;
* explain why maximum likelihood fails for perfect and zero scores;
* convert sum scores to IRT scores with a conversion table;
* read a Wright map;
* estimate how often people are classified on the wrong side of a cut score.
</div>

**Key terms:**
[person score](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#person-score),
[EAP](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#eap),
[MAP](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#map),
[ML](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#ml-scoring),
[WLE](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#wle),
[Wright map](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#wright-map),
[classification accuracy](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#classification-accuracy).

## The ideas

Once the item parameters are known, we can estimate each person's $\theta$
from their responses. The **likelihood** of a response pattern, viewed as a
function of $\theta$, is the product of the item probabilities: $P_j(\theta)$
for each item answered correctly and $1 - P_j(\theta)$ for each item answered
wrongly. The four common estimators use it differently.

* **ML** (maximum likelihood) takes the $\theta$ that maximizes the
  likelihood. It uses only the responses, which makes it attractive for
  fairness arguments, but it does not exist for all-correct or all-wrong
  patterns (the likelihood keeps rising towards $\pm\infty$), and it is
  biased outwards for short tests.
* **WLE** (weighted likelihood, @warm1989) adds a small correction that
  removes most of ML's bias and gives finite estimates for perfect patterns.
* **MAP** (maximum a posteriori) multiplies the likelihood by a prior
  distribution for $\theta$, usually the population distribution, and takes
  the mode of the result.
* **EAP** (expected a posteriori) takes the *mean* of that posterior. It is
  easy to compute, always finite and has the smallest average error, which is
  why it is mirt's default. Like MAP, it **shrinks** estimates towards the
  population mean, more so when the test is short.

The standard error of an EAP estimate is the standard deviation of the
posterior, and it comes for free.

For the Rasch model the sum score carries all the information about
$\theta$, so everyone with the same sum score gets the same estimate. For the
2PL and 3PL, two people with the same sum score can get different estimates,
because correct answers to steep items count for more. Some programmes still
want one score per sum score. **EAP for sum scores** (`method = "EAPsum"`)
gives exactly that, and produces a conversion table that can be printed in a
manual.

## Example 1: Four estimators, one short test

With only five items, the differences between estimators are easy to see.

```{r data-scoring-1}
# Five dichotomous LSAT items, one row per test taker.
resp <- expand.table(LSAT7)
```

```{r}
mod <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
patterns <- unique(resp)
est <- sapply(c("EAP", "MAP", "ML", "WLE"), function(m)
  fscores(mod, method = m, response.pattern = patterns)[, "F1"])
scored <- data.frame(pattern = apply(patterns, 1, paste, collapse = ""),
                     sum = rowSums(patterns), round(est, 2))
scored[order(scored$sum, scored$EAP), ][c(1:4, 15:18, 29:32), ]
```

Read the table from top to bottom. For the all-wrong pattern ML gives
`-Inf`, and for the all-correct pattern `Inf`; WLE, MAP and EAP give finite
values. EAP and MAP are pulled towards zero compared with ML and WLE. And
patterns with the same sum score get different scores under the 2PL,
because Item.3 (the steepest) counts for more than Item.5.

The sum-score conversion table:

```{r}
fscores(mod, method = "EAPsum", full.scores = FALSE)
```

`gg_scores()` shows the distribution of the estimated scores, and
`gg_wright()` puts people and items on the same scale. With five easy items
the Wright map shows the problem at once: The items sit low on the scale,
where few people need to be measured.

```{r scores-wright, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "Distribution of the estimated scores (left) and the Wright map of people and items (right) for LSAT7."}
gg_scores(mod) + gg_wright(mod)
```

## Example 2: A proficiency cut on a mathematics test

We simulate a 40-item end-of-year mathematics test for 2,000 students. The
province calls students at or above $\theta = 0.8$ *proficient*. Because the
data are simulated we know each student's true $\theta$, so we can see how
often the estimates put students on the wrong side of the cut.

```{r data-scoring-2}
# Simulated 40-item mathematics test; true_theta is known for checking.
set.seed(707)
true_theta <- rnorm(2000)
a <- matrix(rlnorm(40, 0.1, 0.25)); b <- rnorm(40, 0, 1)
resp <- simdata(a, matrix(-a * b), N = 2000, itemtype = "2PL",
                Theta = matrix(true_theta))
colnames(resp) <- sprintf("M%02d", 1:40)
```

```{r}
mod <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
eap <- fscores(mod, method = "EAP", full.scores.SE = TRUE)
wle <- fscores(mod, method = "WLE", full.scores.SE = TRUE)
c(cor_eap = cor(eap[, 1], true_theta), cor_wle = cor(wle[, 1], true_theta),
  sd_eap = sd(eap[, 1]), sd_wle = sd(wle[, 1]))
```

With 40 items both estimators correlate about 0.95 with the true values,
and they rank students almost identically. The EAP scores have a smaller
spread than the true values (whose standard deviation is 1) and the WLE
scores a slightly larger one: Shrinkage on one side, measurement error on
the other.

Now the classification. A student is classified correctly if the estimate
and the true value fall on the same side of the cut.

```{r}
cut <- 0.8
truth <- true_theta >= cut
observed <- eap[, 1] >= cut
table(true = truth, estimated = observed)
mean(truth == observed)
```

In practice we never know the truth, but we can estimate the accuracy from
the scores and their standard errors [@rudner2001]. If a student's posterior
is roughly normal with mean $\hat\theta$ and standard deviation
$SE(\hat\theta)$, the probability that their true $\theta$ is above the cut
is $1 - \Phi\left((c - \hat\theta)/SE\right)$. Averaging the probability of
the side they were classified on gives the expected accuracy:

```{r}
p_above <- pnorm((eap[, 1] - cut) / eap[, 2])
expected_accuracy <- mean(ifelse(observed, p_above, 1 - p_above))
expected_accuracy
```

The estimate is close to the accuracy we observed against the truth. The
misclassified students are, of course, the ones near the cut:

```{r misclassified, fig.height = 3.4, fig.cap = "True and estimated ability on the mathematics test; misclassified students lie near the cut."}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data.frame(true = true_theta, est = eap[, 1], wrong = truth != observed),
       aes(true, est, colour = wrong)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = cut, linetype = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = cut, linetype = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey60", `TRUE` = "#C0392B"),
                      labels = c("correct", "misclassified")) +
  labs(x = "True theta", y = "EAP estimate", colour = NULL) +
  theme_mirtverse()
```

`augment()` returns the scores, their standard errors and the response data
as one table, ready to export:

```{r}
head(augment(mod)[, c("M01", "M02", ".F1", ".se_F1")])
```

## Your turn

<div class="yourturn">
1. In Example 1, find two response patterns with a sum score of 3 that get
   different EAP scores. Which items explain the difference?
2. Fit the Rasch model to `LSAT7` and repeat the EAP table. Do patterns with
   the same sum score still get different scores?
3. In Example 2, compute the expected classification accuracy using only the
   first 15 items. How much does it drop?
4. A parent asks why their child, who got 30 of 40 right, has a lower score
   than a classmate who also got 30 right. Write a short answer.
</div>

<details><summary>Solutions</summary>

```{r}
subset(scored, sum == 3)

rasch <- mirt(expand.table(LSAT7), 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE)
r_eap <- fscores(rasch, response.pattern = patterns)[, "F1"]
tapply(round(r_eap, 4), rowSums(patterns), function(x) length(unique(x)))

short <- mirt(resp[, 1:15], 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
e15 <- fscores(short, full.scores.SE = TRUE)
p15 <- pnorm((e15[, 1] - cut) / e15[, 2])
mean(ifelse(e15[, 1] >= cut, p15, 1 - p15))
```

2. No: Under the Rasch model every pattern with the same sum score gets the
   same estimate.
4. For example: "The test gives more weight to questions that are better at
   telling apart students who have mastered the material from those who have
   not. Your child and their classmate answered different questions
   correctly, so their scores differ slightly even though their number
   correct is the same."

</details>

## Further reading {-}

Embretson and Reise [-@embretson2000] compare the scoring methods; Warm
[-@warm1989] introduced the weighted likelihood estimator; Rudner
[-@rudner2001] the approach to expected classification accuracy used here.
